To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
levels of certain miRNAs are different in athletes of different training modalities, and that these levels are probably unrelated to fat or muscle mass.
plasma levels of miR-222 are higher in endurance athletes compared with strength athletes and that plasma levels of several other miRNAs are higher in endurance compared with strength athletes.
levels of certain c-miRNas are different between endurance- and strength-trained athletes, and these c-miRNA may have potential as biomarkers of exercise mode-specific training adaptation.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of microRNAs (miRs) in exercise and training. miRs are small RNA molecules that regulate gene expression by binding to the messenger RNAs of target genes. miRs are present in the circulation and can be used as biomarkers for various diseases, but little is known about their role in exercise and training adaptations.
identifying c-miRNas that may be used to monitor training status in elite athletes.
the discovery and validation of novel biomarkers of exercise and exercise training and the role of c-miRNas in the adaptation to exercise training.

the c-miRNA profile of endurance athletes differs from that of strength athletes, and that the miRNAs miR-222 and miR-146 are potential biomarkers for exercise modality.

the c-miRNomes differ between endurance- versus resistance-trained athletes and are related to exercise mode-specific adaptations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the miRNA profile is a reflection of the training modality and not the muscle bulk or fat mass.
the c-miRNA profiles of the two groups of athletes are different and this difference is probably related to the different training modalities.
